name: Saint Lucia
summary_text: Saint Lucia decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 29 July 2025, when the High Court struck down colonial-era buggery and gross indecency offences as unconstitutional in Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia. Human Rights Watch reported the judgment on 31 July 2025. The case formed part of strategic constitutional litigation across the Eastern Caribbean. For visitors, criminal exposure for private consensual adult same-sex conduct ended with that declaration.  Under Criminal Code No. 9 of 2004, effective 1 January 2005, as amended following the ruling, Section 132 defines gross indecency as genital acts other than intercourse for sexual arousal or gratification. It carries 10 years on indictment or 5 years summarily, but exempts private consensual acts between adults. Section 133 defines buggery as anal intercourse. It carries life imprisonment where committed by force without consent, 10 years in other cases, and 5 years for attempt or assault with intent, but exempts private consensual acts where both persons are 16 or older.  Before the court struck down the provisions, the buggery and gross indecency laws were described as unenforced. Statements in 2017 said no person had been imprisoned for being gay and that gay cruises, couples and visitors stayed safely.  A human rights sensitisation programme for enforcement officers began in 2014 for the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force on general and LGBT-specific content. Further training was held in Castries on 19 May 2015 for officers from the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and Bordelais Correctional Facility, together with CariFLAGS, the Canadian HIV-AIDS Legal Network and Maurice Tomlinson, building on the 2014 work.  Two incidents of anti-gay violence are documented. In 2011, three American gay men were violently attacked and robbed in a vacation villa by assailants who used anti-gay slurs. In February 2019, 27-year-old Guyanese national Michael Pooran was stabbed to death in an attack attributed to perceived sexual orientation, which prompted public calls to denounce violence and discrimination and to re-examine the buggery laws.

name: Liechtenstein
summary_text: Same-sex sexual relations are lawful in Liechtenstein.  Anti-discrimination law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not covered by any anti-discrimination statute in force.  Protection on grounds of sexual orientation includes criminal prohibitions. Since 1 April 2016 harassment and incitement to hatred on grounds of sexual orientation have been banned. Section 283(1) of the Penal Code punishes public incitement to hatred or discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation with imprisonment of up to two years. Section 283(6) prohibits discrimination in public facilities on grounds including sexual orientation.  No procedure exists for changing a legal gender marker in official documents.  No law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity.  Civil marriage and joint adoption have been available to same-sex couples since January 2025.
